titolo: Questo suono sale per 14 secondi e finisce esattamente dove era partito 🔁 #shorts
descrizione:
È la scala di Shepard (Roger Shepard, 1964; la versione continua è di Jean-Claude Risset): ogni nota è fatta di più ottave insieme. Quelle in alto svaniscono, quelle in basso rientrano piano, e il cervello segue solo la salita.

È il trucco dietro le scale infinite di Super Mario 64 e, come ha raccontato Christopher Nolan, dietro la tensione continua della colonna sonora di Dunkirk.

Nei tuoi brani: un riser costruito così crea tensione senza mai arrivare al picco.

Riascoltalo e trova il punto in cui ricomincia. Poi mandalo a chi giura di avere l'orecchio assoluto 👇

Quando si spegne, nel video c'è silenzio vero, eppure molte persone sentono per qualche secondo una nota debole, vicina al bordo basso di quel buco. Non succede a tutti. Meglio in cuffia, a volume medio, al buio.

titolo: In cuffia: da dove arrivava il loop la seconda volta? 🎧 #shorts

Il volume era identico nei due orecchi e non ho toccato il pan. Ho solo fatto arrivare la destra 8 millisecondi dopo: il cervello fonde i due suoni e li mette dal lato di quello che arriva prima. Oltre una certa soglia, invece, li separa e senti un'eco.

È l'effetto Haas (o della precedenza), dal nome di Helmut Haas, 1951. Nel mix si usa per allargare: doppia una chitarra e ritarda una copia di 10-20 ms. Ma controlla sempre in mono, perché sommate le due copie si cancellano a certe frequenze.

Salvalo per il prossimo mix e mandalo a chi allarga tutto col pan 👇

Prima di giudicare un plugin, pareggia il volume e confronta a occhi chiusi.

titolo: Lo stesso pezzetto di rumore, ripetuto più in fretta, diventa una nota 🎹 #shorts
descrizione:
Il suono non cambia mai: è sempre lo stesso rumore, ripetuto in loop sempre più corto. Una volta al secondo è un fruscio, dieci volte è un ritmo, cento volte è una nota. Sopra le 20-30 ripetizioni al secondo il cervello smette di contarle e sente un'altezza.

È il rumore ripetuto studiato da Guttman e Julesz (1963). Per chi produce: un loop cortissimo di qualsiasi suono è già un synth. Provalo col tuo sampler.

Ogni coppia sono due note a mezza ottava esatta, fatte solo di ottave sovrapposte: non hanno un'altezza precisa, quindi è il tuo cervello a decidere se la seconda è sopra o sotto. Persone diverse sentono direzioni opposte.

È il paradosso del tritono, scoperto da Diana Deutsch nel 1986. Nel 1991 ha mostrato che conta anche la lingua con cui sei cresciuto: californiani e inglesi del sud tendevano a sentire direzioni opposte.

titolo: Metti le cuffie: da che lato hai sentito la nota acuta? 🎧 #shorts
descrizione:
In realtà l'acuta salta da un orecchio all'altro ogni quarto di secondo, e lo stesso fa la grave. Il cervello prende l'altezza da un orecchio e la posizione dall'altro, e ti fa sentire una combinazione che nelle cuffie non c'è.

È l'illusione dell'ottava, scoperta da Diana Deutsch nel 1974. Secondo le sue ricerche, chi è destrimane tende a sentire l'acuta a destra.

descrizione:
È l'illusione "speech-to-song", scoperta dalla psicologa Diana Deutsch nel 1995: ripeti identica una frase parlata e, dopo qualche giro, il cervello smette di seguire il significato e ascolta solo le altezze della voce. La melodia c'era già.

Nei tuoi brani funziona con un sample vocale in loop: dopo qualche ripetizione diventa un ritornello.

titolo: The same tiny piece of noise, repeated faster, becomes a note 🎹 #shorts
descrizione:
The sound never changes: it's always the same noise, looped shorter and shorter. Once per second it's a hiss, ten times is a rhythm, a hundred times is a note. Above 20-30 repetitions per second your brain stops counting them and hears a pitch.

It's the repeated noise studied by Guttman and Julesz (1963). For producers: a super short loop of any sound is already a synth. Try it on your sampler.

It never stops, because it isn't really speeding up: it's many layers of the same beat, each one twice as fast as the other. As they speed up, the fastest fade out and the slowest fade in, so your ear only follows the ones that are accelerating.

It's the Risset rhythm, the rhythmic twin of the endless scale (Jean-Claude Risset).

descrizione:
It's always two notes alternating, high and low, in a gallop rhythm. Slowly it's one gallop. As it speeds up, your brain stops following them as one melody and splits them into two rhythms: one above, one below. The notes never change.

It's auditory stream segregation (Leon van Noorden, 1975). Bach used it to make a single violin sound like two voices.

titolo: This sound rises for 14 seconds and ends exactly where it started 🔁 #shorts
descrizione:
It's the Shepard tone (Roger Shepard, 1964; the continuous version is by Jean-Claude Risset): every note is several octaves at once. The top ones fade out, the bottom ones sneak back in, and your brain only follows the climb.

It's the trick behind the endless stairs in Super Mario 64 and, as Christopher Nolan has explained, behind the nonstop tension in the Dunkirk score.

In your tracks: a riser built this way builds tension without ever peaking.

titolo: Headphones on: where was the loop coming from the second time? 🎧 #shorts
descrizione:
The volume was identical in both ears and I didn't touch the pan. I just made the right side arrive 8 milliseconds later: your brain fuses the two sounds and places them on the side of whichever arrives first. Past a certain point, though, it splits them and you hear an echo.

It's the Haas effect (or precedence effect), named after Helmut Haas, 1951. In a mix it's used for width: double a guitar and delay one copy by 10-20 ms. But always check in mono, because summed together the two copies cancel out at some frequencies.

Save it for your next mix and send it to someone who widens everything with the pan 👇

titolo: Up or down? Write it before reading, for the first and second pair 👇 #shorts
descrizione:
Each pair is two notes exactly half an octave apart, made only of stacked octaves: they have no exact pitch, so your brain decides whether the second one is above or below. Different people hear opposite directions.

It's the tritone paradox, discovered by Diana Deutsch in 1986. In 1991 she showed that even the language you grew up with matters: Californians and people from southern England tended to hear opposite directions.

Send it to a friend and ask what they hear: you probably won't agree.

titolo: How many beeps did you hear at the start? They were always there, same volume 🔇 #shorts
descrizione:
It's masking: when two sounds share the same frequencies, the louder one covers the other. In the video I didn't turn the beeps up, I just removed the noise around their frequency. MP3 uses the same principle to save space: it throws away what you wouldn't hear anyway.

In a mix it happens to vocals and guitars: instead of turning everything up, make room with subtractive EQ, a high-pass or sidechain.

In reality the high note jumps from one ear to the other every quarter of a second, and so does the low one. Your brain takes the pitch from one ear and the position from the other, and makes you hear a combination that isn't in the headphones.

It's the octave illusion, discovered by Diana Deutsch in 1974. According to her research, right-handed people tend to hear the high note on the right.

Put your headphones on. Both ears get the exact same noise, but on the right I flipped a very thin slice of frequencies, note by note. On its own, each ear only hears hiss. Together, your brain compares the two sides and the difference becomes a melody that exists in neither.

It's called Huggins pitch (Cramer and Huggins, 1958). You won't hear it from a phone speaker, and if you take one side off it disappears. Not everyone catches it right away: turn it up a bit and listen again.

In a mix it works like this: a saturated copy of the bass adds harmonics and makes it come through even on small speakers.

It's the same trick as Yanny/Laurel: faced with a sound that's missing pieces, your brain picks the most likely guess.

titolo: When did you start hearing it sing? Third time? Fifth? 🔁 #shorts
descrizione:
It's the speech-to-song illusion, discovered by psychologist Diana Deutsch in 1995: repeat a spoken phrase exactly and, after a few loops, your brain stops following the meaning and listens only to the pitch of the voice. The melody was already there.

In your tracks it works with a looped vocal sample: after a few repeats it becomes a hook.

Play it again from the start: the first phrase sings now. At which repetition did it happen for you? 👇

titolo: You know this song, but you can't name it 🎹 #shorts
descrizione:
Every note is the right one, but each is played in a random octave. Almost nobody recognizes the song, because your brain finds a melody by its ups and downs, and those are gone.

Diana Deutsch tested this in 1972: people barely recognized famous tunes with scrambled octaves. Once they knew the title, they heard it.

Did you get it before the reveal? Send it to a friend and don't tell them the title 👇

titolo: How high can you still hear? 8,000 to 19,000 Hz 🎧 #shorts
descrizione:
Headphones on, start at low volume. Pure tones climb from 8,000 to 19,000 Hz. Comment the last number you can hear 👇

The cells that hear the highest pitches sit at the entrance of the cochlea and wear out first: with age, and faster with loud music. Phone speakers, cheap earbuds and compression can cut the top too, so try good headphones.

Send it to a friend: who hears higher?

titolo: Where is this sound: in front, behind or above you? 🎧 #shorts
descrizione:
Headphones on, eyes closed. Three sounds, A, B and C. They're all in the same spot: the same sound in both ears, only the pitch band changes.

Your outer ear colours sound differently from every direction, so your brain reads the band as a direction. For most people A (4 kHz) is in front, B (1 kHz) behind, C (8 kHz) above. Jens Blauert found these "directional bands" in 1969.

Where did you hear them? Send it to a friend and compare 👇

titolo: One note or two? Comment the number where you hear two 🎧 #shorts
descrizione:
Five sounds, same note every time, built from 10 pitches. From sound 2 on, one of them is pushed out of tune: 1%, 2%, 4%, 8%. At some point your brain stops counting it as part of the note and you hear a separate tone.

In the 1986 study by Moore, Glasberg and Peters it usually happened between 1% and 3%, and it changed from person to person. It's one of the ways your ears tell two instruments apart.

At which number did you hear two? Send it to a friend and compare 👇

titolo: Does this tone ever stop? Your brain says no 🎧 #shorts
descrizione:
A is a gliding tone full of silent gaps: you hear it break. B is the same tone with the gaps filled by bursts of noise, and most people hear it keep going.

Under every burst there was silence. A loud noise could have hidden the tone, so your brain assumes it kept going and fills in the missing pieces. It's auditory induction (Warren, Obusek & Ackroff, 1972), the same trick that lets you follow a voice in a noisy room.

Did you hear it continue? Send it to a friend 👇
